analysis.one_liner: Lowers federal sugar price supports and import limits to reduce US sugar prices.
analysis.headline: Sixteen senators — 10 Democrats and 6 Republicans — sponsored this sugar price reform, and it died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would scale back the federal sugar program: it cuts the price floor the government guarantees sugar growers, repeals the caps on how much sugar producers can sell in the US market, sets sugar import quotas at the minimum allowed under trade agreements, and repeals a program that pays bioenergy plants to buy surplus sugar. These controls are what keep US sugar prices well above world prices, so the changes would tend to cut costs for households and food makers while reducing growers' guaranteed returns. The bill was introduced with bipartisan backing and then sat untouched in the Agriculture Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: American households and sugar-using food and beverage manufacturers, who pay a premium for sugar because the current program holds domestic prices well above world levels through price supports, sales limits, and import quotas. Taxpayers also gain, because the bill repeals the Feedstock Flexibility Program, which spends public money paying bioenergy producers to buy surplus sugar so growers do not default on federal loans.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the price-support loan rate the Agriculture Department guarantees to sugar growers for the 2021 through 2025 crop years, lowering the government-backed floor under sugar prices.
Repeals the marketing allotments that cap how much sugar each processor may sell in the domestic market, which would increase the supply of sugar available to American buyers.

Sets sugar import quotas at the minimum required by US trade agreements and directs the Agriculture Department to adjust them so supplies are adequate and prices are reasonable, weighing the effects on consumers, workers, businesses, and small businesses.
Repeals the Feedstock Flexibility Program, ending a taxpayer-funded program that pays bioenergy producers to buy surplus sugar so it does not get dumped on the government.

analysis.who_pays: Sugar beet and cane growers and processors — a few thousand farms and a handful of companies concentrated in states like Florida, Louisiana, Minnesota, and North Dakota — would receive lower guaranteed prices and face more import competition. Taxpayers, by contrast, would save money by ending the bioenergy sugar-buying program.

drawbacks.text: The bill strips away the price floor, sales limits, and import restrictions that keep US sugar growers profitable, exposing growers concentrated in a handful of beet- and cane-growing states to lower prices and foreign competition, and some could not survive the change.

Defenders of the current program have long argued that foreign sugar producers face lower costs and receive subsidies of their own, so opening the US market could shift production overseas rather than deliver lasting price relief; this bill contained no transition aid for growers who would absorb that shock.

Even after this reform, the government would still manage the sugar market — import quotas would remain at trade-agreement minimums, the Agriculture Department would target a 15.5 percent stocks-to-use ratio, and price-support loans would continue — so this is a smaller government role, not a free market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad but diffuse: every household and food manufacturer that buys sugar pays the premium the current program charges, while the costs fall on a small, concentrated group of growers who have organized effectively to protect it. On the merits, the consumers-and-taxpayers side of the ledger is much larger than the growers' side, and even this bill would have softened the transition by keeping import quotas and price-support loans in place. The serious objection is fairness to growers during a shift to lower prices, and the bill offered them nothing to cushion it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jeanne Shaheen introduced the bill on July 26, 2021, with 15 cosponsors split between 9 Democrats and 6 Republicans, ranging from Elizabeth Warren to Marsha Blackburn.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US sugar growers and processors came out ahead: they kept the price supports, sales limits, and import quotas that hold US sugar prices above world levels, and consumers kept paying the difference.

for.name: Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the sugar price supports and import limits that raise US sugar prices, and recruited 15 bipartisan cosponsors.

for.name: 9 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senators Casey, Coons, Durbin, Hassan, Kaine, Markey, Menendez, Warner, and Warren.

for.name: 6 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senators Toomey, Blackburn, Collins, Johnson, Portman, and Young.

against.name: Debbie Stabenow
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in her committee from July 2021 until the Congress ended with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled.

against.name: American Sugar Alliance
against.role: Sugar growers' and processors' trade association
against.what_they_did: Longstanding defender of the sugar price support, allotment, and import quota system, and consistent opponent of sugar program reform bills like this one.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 10 Democrats and 6 Republicans, spanning from Elizabeth Warren to Marsha Blackburn — and the bill was stopped by committee inaction rather than a party-line vote; the program's defenders have historically come from sugar-growing states in both parties.

industries.industry: Sugar beet and cane growers and processors
industries.note: The federal program holds US sugar prices well above world levels through guaranteed price floors, caps on domestic sales, and import quotas, and this bill would have lowered the floor, freed sales, and opened imports. Growers' revenue depends on the premium American consumers pay, so their interest runs directly against sugar buyers.

Sugar is a major input for candy, cereal, baked goods, and beverage makers, so lower US sugar prices would cut their costs and their prices. The bill specifically directs the Agriculture Department to weigh effects on businesses and small businesses when setting import levels.
The Feedstock Flexibility Program pays bioenergy plants to buy surplus sugar so it never gets forfeited to the government; repealing it ends that taxpayer-funded revenue stream.

industries.industry: Sugar importers and foreign sugar producers
industries.note: Setting import quotas at the minimum required by trade agreements, rather than the discretionary levels USDA now sets, would allow substantially more foreign sugar into the US market.
